guide.title: Period 8 (1945–1980): review guide
guide.intro: After World War II the United States led a global struggle against communism while experiencing unprecedented prosperity at home. Civil rights movements, the Great Society, the Vietnam War, and new social movements challenged and changed American society. Continuity and change is the period's key reasoning skill.

sections.title: The Cold War, the Red Scare, and Vietnam
body: Containment of Soviet communism guided policy: the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan, NATO (1949), the Korean War (1950–1953), and a nuclear arms race. Fear of communist subversion fed a Red Scare, including Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations.

U.S. involvement in Vietnam grew after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964). The Tet Offensive (1968) shook public confidence, and a growing antiwar movement, including veterans, questioned the war. U.S. combat involvement ended in 1973.
points: Containment shaped foreign policy from Truman through the 1970s.
Vietnam divided Americans and weakened trust in government.

sections.title: Civil rights movements
body: Early steps included the desegregation of the armed forces (1948) and Brown v. Board of Education (1954). Nonviolent direct action, from the Montgomery bus boycott (1955–1956) to sit-ins and the March on Washington (1963), helped win the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Some activists later embraced Black Power and more militant approaches.
The movement inspired others: Latino, American Indian, Asian American, women's, and gay rights activists organized for equality.
points: Courts, Congress, and grassroots activism all mattered.
Divisions grew within the movement over tactics and goals.

sections.title: Prosperity, culture, the Great Society, and transition
body: Postwar prosperity, the GI Bill, suburbanization, and the baby boom produced a mass consumer culture, though critics questioned conformity and many cities and minorities were left out. Lyndon Johnson's Great Society (Medicare, Medicaid, the War on Poverty, federal aid to education) expanded the federal role.

In the 1960s, a youth counterculture challenged traditional values; environmental concerns grew (Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, 1962; the EPA, 1970). In the 1970s, Watergate, energy crises, and stagflation undercut confidence, and a conservative reaction began to build.
points: Continuity and change: liberal government expanded in the 1960s and faced a backlash in the 1970s.
Prosperity was real but unevenly shared.

example.prompt: Explain how the Truman Doctrine reflected the policy of containment.
example.solution: Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey to keep them from falling to communism, committing the United States to support free peoples resisting communist pressure, which became the basis of containing Soviet influence.

misconceptions: It built on decades of earlier activism, legal challenges, and wartime gains.
“Containment meant war with the Soviet Union.”
It aimed to stop communism's spread without direct war between the superpowers.
Veterans, clergy, and many others also opposed the war.
Many in cities, rural areas, and minority communities were left out.

passages.title: Source A: President Harry Truman, address to Congress, 1947
text: “At the present moment in world history nearly every nation must choose between alternative ways of life. The choice is too often not a free one. Should we fail to aid Greece and Turkey in this fateful hour, the effect will be far reaching to the West as well as to the East. The seeds of totalitarian regimes are nurtured by misery and want. They spread and grow in the evil soil of poverty and strife. They reach their full growth when the hope of a people for a better life has died. We must keep that hope alive.”
passages.attribution: President Harry S. Truman, address to a joint session of Congress requesting aid to Greece and Turkey, March 12, 1947. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 28.2.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/28-2-the-cold-war); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Testimony of John Kerry, Vietnam Veterans Against the War, 1971
text: “I would like to talk on behalf of all those veterans and say that several months ago in Detroit we had an investigation at which over 150 honorably discharged, and many very highly decorated, veterans testified to war crimes committed in Southeast Asia. . . . We could come back to this country, we could be quiet, we could hold our silence, we could not tell what went on in Vietnam, but we feel because of what threatens this country, not the reds [Communists], but the crimes which we are committing that threaten it, that we have to speak out.”
passages.attribution: John Kerry, a former U.S. Navy lieutenant and member of Vietnam Veterans Against the War, testifying before the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, April 1971. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 30.3.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/30-3-vietnam-the-downward-spiral); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the civil rights movement
text: “The victories of the mid-1960s rested on decades of work. Lawyers for the NAACP spent years building the cases that led to Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. Ordinary people, from the bus riders of Montgomery to the student sit-in activists of 1960, used nonviolent protest to expose segregation to a national audience. Their pressure helped produce the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which, along with Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs, marked the high point of federal action for racial and economic equality.”

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of postwar suburbs
text: “Nothing symbolized postwar prosperity more than the suburb. Federally insured mortgages and the GI Bill let millions of families buy new homes, and highways carried them to work in the cities they had left. Yet the suburbs were not open to everyone: lending rules and local practices kept most Black families out, even as the industries and tax revenues that had supported city neighborhoods moved away. The suburban boom helped build a large middle class and, at the same time, deepened racial divisions in American metropolitan areas.”
